planting.note: Pot up rhizome divisions any time indoors; move containers to a shaded porch only after all frost danger has passed.

directions: Grow in a loose, fast-draining mix and keep the rhizome surface slightly above soil level to prevent rot. Let the top inch of substrate dry between waterings and avoid wetting the pink-and-cream foliage directly. Divide congested rhizomes in spring to create new starts. Bright, filtered light keeps leaf coloring crisp without scorching.

planting.note: Pot divisions in rich, moisture-retentive soil; this swamp aroid is far more water-tolerant than most houseplant Alocasia relatives.

directions: This marsh-dwelling aroid wants constantly damp to boggy soil, so it can sit in a saucer of standing water during active growth. Pink leaf veining is most vivid under bright, dappled shade. Give it room to size up, since mature specimens form a sizable arrow-shaped leaf canopy. Repot every year or two as the rhizome bulks up.

planting.note: Root 2-3 segment stem cuttings in barely damp mix; set finished plants outdoors in summer shade before bringing them in ahead of fall frost.

directions: Unlike desert cacti, this epiphyte wants a well-drained but humus-rich mix that never fully dries out during active growth. Bright, filtered light keeps the flattened stem segments from reddening with stress. Give it cool nights and shortening days in autumn to trigger the holiday-season flower buds. Avoid moving the plant once buds have set, since bud drop follows sudden light or temperature changes.

planting.note: Divide the fleshy crown in spring and pot into a light, peat-based mix.

directions: Bright, indirect light produces the heaviest flower count without bleaching the strap-shaped leaves. Water from below when the surface is dry to the touch, and avoid splashing the crown, which can cause rot. Remove spent blooms promptly to keep flushes coming through most of the year.

planting.note: Separate offset rosettes from the parent crown and pot individually into a light, open mix.

directions: Grow under bright, filtered light to encourage the ruffled-edge blooms to open fully. Feed with a dilute, phosphorus-leaning fertilizer during the growing season to sustain repeat flowering. Keep air circulating around the dense leaf rosette to prevent mildew in humid rooms.

common_name: Bold Belles Dappled Morning Angel Wing Begonia

planting.note: Root stem cuttings indoors; move finished plants to a shaded porch display once nights stay above 55F.

directions: Silver-spotted, wing-shaped leaves and clustered pink flowers both benefit from bright, filtered light that avoids midday sun. Allow the soil to dry slightly between thorough waterings to discourage the stem rot that cane-type begonias are prone to. Pinch young plants to encourage branching, since unpinched canes grow tall and sparse.

common_name: Bold Belles Criss Cross Iron Cross Begonia

planting.note: Divide rhizomes when repotting in spring; grow in shade year-round as the puckered foliage scorches easily.

directions: The textured, puckered leaves carry a dark cross-shaped marking that stays most pronounced in low, even light. Keep humidity on the higher side, since the quilted leaf surface can brown at the edges in dry indoor air. Let the rhizome creep across the pot surface rather than burying it when repotting.

planting.note: Set out transplants after all danger of frost, into a shaded bed or container that stays reliably moist.

directions: Deep purple-and-gold wishbone-shaped flowers keep blooming through summer heat as long as the roots never dry out completely. This torenia thrives in spots too shady for most flowering annuals, including under tree canopies. Deadheading is not required, since spent flowers are hidden by new growth, but a light trim mid-season keeps plants compact.
